passages.text: Feasibility of Training a Random Forest Model With Incomplete User-Specific Data for Devising a Control Strategy for Active Biomimetic Ankle

Intelligent control strategies for active biomimetic prostheses could exploit the inter-joint coordination of limbs in human gait in order to mimic the functioning of a biological joint. <sentence_start/>A machine learning regression model could be employed to learn an input-output relationship between the coordinated limb motion in human gait and predict the motion of a particular limb/joint given the motion of other limbs/joints. <sentence_start/>Such a model could be potentially used as a controller for an intelligent prosthesis which aims to restore the functioning similar to an intact biological joint. <sentence_start/>For this, the model needs to be tailored for each user by learning the gait pattern specific to the user. <sentence_start/>The challenge of training such machine learning regression models in prosthetic control is that, the desired reference output cannot be obtained from an amputee due to the missing limb. <sentence_start/>In this study, we investigate the feasibility of using two different methods for training a random forest algorithm using incomplete amputee-specific data to predict the ankle kinematics and dynamics from hip, knee, and shank kinematics. <sentence_start/>First is an inter-subject approach which learns a generalized input-output relationship from a group of able-bodied individuals and then applies this generalized relationship to amputees. <sentence_start/>Second is a subject-specific approach which maps the amputee's inputs to a desired normative reference output calculated from able-bodied individuals. <sentence_start/>The subject-specific model outperformed the inter-subject model in predicting the ankle angle and moment in most cases and can be potentially used for devising a control strategy for an intelligent biomimetic ankle.
1. Introduction

Lower limb amputation hinders the quality of life. <sentence_start/>The passive replacements of a missing limb are incapable of restoring normal gait (Varol and Goldfarb, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICORR.2007.4428514" count="1">2007</citation>; Windrich et al., <citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12938-016-0284-9" pmid="28105948" pmcid="PMC5249019" count="1">2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>Active or intelligent biomimetic prostheses that are actuated using embedded motors can better support natural gait by substituting the missing muscle function and providing adequate torque (Varol and Goldfarb, <citation rid="B40" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICORR.2007.4428514" count="1">2007</citation>; Windrich et al., <citation rid="B44" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/s12938-016-0284-9" pmid="28105948" pmcid="PMC5249019" count="1">2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>The central unit of such active prostheses is an intelligent control strategy that interprets the user's locomotive intention from the residual limb motion (Villarreal et al., <citation rid="B42" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TNSRE.2016.2569019" pmid="27187967" pmcid="PMC5107364" count="1">2016</citation>; Bartlett and Goldfarb, <citation rid="B5" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TBME.2017.2750139" pmid="28910754" count="1">2017</citation>) and thereby actuate the prosthetic joints to enable the desired locomotion similar to that of able-bodied individuals'. <sentence_start/>To define appropriate control strategy for such active prostheses, the functioning of a biological joint during human gait can be mimicked. <sentence_start/>A machine learning regression model could be employed to learn an input-output relationship between the coordinated limb motion in human gait (Boudali et al., <citation rid="B8" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/EMBC.2017.8037216" pmid="29060260" count="1">2017</citation>) and predict the motion of a particular limb/joint given the motion of other limbs/joints. <sentence_start/>Such a model could be potentially used as a controller for an intelligent prosthesis which aims to restore the functioning similar to an intact biological joint.

The development of a control strategy for active prostheses can be achieved in four stages: (1) selecting the control model, (2) selecting model input features, (3) selecting model outputs, and (4) establishing an input-output relationship.

The first stage is choosing the control model that translates the user's locomotive intention inferred from sensory input to output commands for actuating the active prosthetic joints. <sentence_start/>Existing control models can be broadly classified as discrete or continuous. <sentence_start/>In the discrete approach, a gait cycle (or a stride) is divided into discrete phases and inputs from external sensors are used to recognize the intended gait phase of a particular locomotion mode (Sup et al., <citation rid="B37" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/0278364907084588" pmid="19898683" pmcid="PMC2773553" count="1">2008</citation>; Varol et al., <citation rid="B41" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TBME.2009.2034734" pmid="19846361" pmcid="PMC2829115" count="1">2010</citation>). <sentence_start/>For each kinematic or kinetic variable (i.e., state) to be controlled, its desirable value is specified by a finite-state controller, which uses a lookup table that corresponds to the recognized gait phase. <sentence_start/>A finer division of the gait cycle as well as an increase in the number of locomotion modes or states to be controlled result in an exponential increase in the number of parameters to be tuned as well as look-up tables to be maintained (Lawson et al., <citation rid="B25" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICRA.2013.6631124" count="1">2013</citation>; Tucker et al., <citation rid="B39" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1743-0003-12-1" pmid="25557982" pmcid="PMC4326520" count="1">2015</citation>). <sentence_start/>On the other hand, in a continuous approach, the prosthesis kinematics or kinetics (state) is continuously varied depending on the sensor input. <sentence_start/>Machine learning regression algorithms have recently received increased attention as a continuous control model for active prostheses (Eslamy and Schilling, <citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/BIOROB.2018.8487213" count="1">2018</citation>; Dey et al., <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICORR.2019.8779445" pmid="31374717" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>Unlike the discrete finite-state models, machine learning regression models can learn a continuous relationship between the sensor input and the output control variables (prosthesis kinetics or kinematics) to be predicted.

The second stage is choosing the input to the control model. <sentence_start/>The input should reflect the user's locomotive intention and enable the model to learn a robust input-output relationship for a given prosthesis user. <sentence_start/>Some of the feasible input choices are residual limb kinematics (Holgate et al., <citation rid="B19" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ROBOT.2009.5152565" count="1">2009</citation>; Quintero et al., <citation rid="B31" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/IROS.2016.7759798" pmcid="PMC5381823" pmid="28392969" count="1">2016</citation>) or muscle activation (Au et al., <citation rid="B4" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICORR.2005.1501123" count="1">2005</citation>; Huang et al., <citation rid="B21" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TBME.2011.2161671" pmid="21768042" pmcid="PMC3235670" count="1">2011</citation>).

The third stage is choosing the outputs of the control model. <sentence_start/>The choice of the outputs depends on what best governs locomotion in specific scenarios [e.g., type of prosthesis, kinematic and kinetic behaviors of the prosthetic joints, balance, or efficiency of gait (Jezernik et al., <citation rid="B23" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1046/j.1525-1403.2003.03017.x" pmid="22150969" count="1">2003</citation>; Au et al., <citation rid="B3" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neunet.2008.03.006" pmid="18499394" count="1">2008</citation>; Eilenberg et al., <citation rid="B14" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TNSRE.2009.2039620" pmid="20071268" count="1">2010</citation>; Tsukahara et al., <citation rid="B38" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/IROS.2011.6094827" count="1">2011</citation>)].

The fourth stage is establishing an appropriate relationship between the selected input features and outputs, such that the control model can realize the desired locomotion. <sentence_start/>This stage is particularly critical to ensure adequate prosthetic control and is the main focus of our study. <sentence_start/>For a machine learning regression model, the aforementioned input-output relationship is established through training. <sentence_start/>The challenge of training the machine learning regression models for active prosthesis control is that the complete training data cannot be obtained from amputees due to the missing limb. <sentence_start/>One way to address this problem is by using an inter-subject approach that seeks a generalized input-output relationship using locomotion data from a group of able-bodied individuals (Ardestani et al., <citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.eswa.2013.11.003" count="1">2014</citation>) and is applied to the prosthetic user. <sentence_start/>The advantage of the inter-subject approach is that, once the generalized input-output relationship is established, the model requires no training data to be collected from the new individual. <sentence_start/>However, an obvious disadvantage is that the prediction accuracy may suffer if the input from a particular individual substantially deviates from the training data due to inter-individual variations in gait (Hof, <citation rid="B18" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0966-6362(95)01057-2" pmid="11323225" count="1">1996</citation>; Stansfield et al., <citation rid="B36" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/S0966-6362(02)00062-0" pmid="12535730" count="1">2003</citation>; Senden et al., <citation rid="B34" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.physio.2011.06.002" pmid="23122438" count="1">2012</citation>; Wahid et al., <citation rid="B43" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1123/jab.2015-0035" pmid="26426798" count="1">2016</citation>; Allard et al., <citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3917/sm.098.0005" count="1">2017</citation>). <sentence_start/>This is especially relevant for prosthetic control, as amputees are more likely to exhibit gait abnormalities (Winter and Sienko, <citation rid="B45" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/0021-9290(88)90142-X" pmid="3417688" count="1">1988</citation>; Silverman et al., <citation rid="B35" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gaitpost.2008.04.005" pmid="18514526" count="1">2008</citation>). <sentence_start/>While some studies suggest to account for the inter-individual variability in gait by scaling the input features (Pinzone et al., <citation rid="B29" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gaitpost.2015.11.013" pmid="27004635" count="1">2016</citation>; Allard et al., <citation rid="B1" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3917/sm.098.0005" count="1">2017</citation>), the parameters for scaling are typically anthropometric and likely not effective in compensating for the inherently different gait patterns across individuals.

Another way to address this could be a subject-specific approach that identifies a unique input-output relationship based on the experimental data from a particular individual (Dey et al., <citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICORR.2019.8779445" pmid="31374717" count="1">2019</citation>). <sentence_start/>However, a subject-specific approach cannot be directly applied for amputees due to the absence of desired reference outputs from the amputee her/himself. <sentence_start/>Hence, to make the subject-specific model applicable for amputees, we used a modified subject-specific approach to learn a relationship between the amputee's input and a normative reference output calculated from a sample of able-bodied subjects' walking trials at a similar speed as that of the amputee. <sentence_start/>The main advantage of this approach is that the input from a specific user need not be similar to that of a group of able-bodied individuals to produce the desired normative output values.

In this study, we assessed the feasibility of training a random forest model with incomplete user-specific data for designing a potential control strategy for an active biomimetic ankle prosthesis. <sentence_start/>To achieve this, we compared the two types of models: inter-subject and the subject-specific, to continuously predict the ankle angles and moments within gait cycles based on random forest regression (Breiman, <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1010933404324" count="1">2001</citation>). <sentence_start/>We chose random forest regression for devising the control model because it possesses characteristics that make it more suitable than other competing algorithms for controlling an active prosthesis. <sentence_start/>First, random forest has demonstrated to give a more robust and accurate prediction performance compared to other algorithms like Gaussian process regression and support vector regression (Hultquist et al., <citation rid="B22" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/2150704X.2014.963733" count="1">2014</citation>). <sentence_start/>Unlike other machine learning models (e.g., the distance-based models), where it is recommended that the features be normalized to attain a high prediction accuracy or a faster convergence (Hsu et al., <citation rid="B20" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2003</citation>; Khah and Wu, <citation rid="B24" ref-type="bibr" count="1">2019</citation>), random forests do not require input feature normalization, which makes it more suitable for real-time usage. <sentence_start/>Additionally, random forests can achieve high prediction accuracy being trained on a small training set and with less training time as opposed to many other machine learning algorithms (Douglas et al., <citation rid="B13" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.neuroimage.2010.11.002" pmid="21073969" pmcid="PMC3099263" count="1">2011</citation>; Biau, <citation rid="B6" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5555/2188385.2343682" count="1">2012</citation>; Biau and Scornet, <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11749-016-0481-7" count="1">2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>As a result, only a minimal amount of data might be required from the amputee for training the prosthesis controller. <sentence_start/>Moreover, random forests are easily parallelizable and hence suitable for dealing with a large amount of training data in real-time (Biau and Scornet, <citation rid="B7" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11749-016-0481-7" count="1">2016</citation>). <sentence_start/>This can come to benefit when updating/learning the model online, to continuously adapt to new training data over time, in order to account for changes in locomotion speeds, patterns, or the prosthetic setup. <sentence_start/>Lastly, random forests can quantify the relative importance of input features in decision making, which can be used for feature selection and dimensionality reduction.

The hip, knee, and shank kinematics were used as input to the random forest models in this study. <sentence_start/>Since the potential utility of the predictions of the models is for controlling a prosthetic ankle joint, the ankle angle and ankle moment were chosen as the output of our models. <sentence_start/>The performance of the inter-subject and subject-specific models were evaluated based on how well the trained models could generate the desired ankle angle and moment for thirty able-bodied subjects walking at five different speeds and two transtibial amputees (below-knee amputated) walking at self-selected comfortable and fast walking speeds. <sentence_start/>Additionally, a feature importance evaluation was performed using random forests to determine the most important features as input to the model in pursuit of reducing the input dimension while maintaining accuracy.
2. Methodology

Random forest models were trained to predict the ankle angle (θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic>) and moment (τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic>) using the ipsilateral hip flexion-extension angle (θ<italic><sub>hip</sub></italic>), knee flexion-extension angle (θ<italic><sub>knee</sub></italic>), shank segment orientation in the sagittal plane (θ<italic><sub>shank</sub></italic>), and their first derivatives . <sentence_start/>The training was performed using two different approaches: inter-subject and subject-specific. <sentence_start/>Normative input and output data were obtained from a publicly-available dataset (Fukuchi et al., <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7717/peerj.4640" pmid="29707431" pmcid="PMC5922232" count="1">2018</citation>) while input data from two unilateral transtibial amputees was obtained experimentally. <sentence_start/>The experimental protocols were approved by the local ethics committee of the University Medical Center Göttingen, Göttingen, Germany (reference number: 26/3/18), and the participants gave their written informed consent before the experiment.
2.1. Subject Selection and Data Acquisition

Normative model inputs (θ<italic><sub>hip</sub></italic>, θ<italic><sub>knee</sub></italic>, and θ<italic><sub>shank</sub></italic>) and outputs (θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> and τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic>) were obtained from a publicly-available dataset (Fukuchi et al., <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7717/peerj.4640" pmid="29707431" pmcid="PMC5922232" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>The data was acquired using a marker-based motion capture system with 12 cameras (Raptor-4; Motion Analysis Corporation, Santa Rosa, CA, USA) and an instrumented treadmill (FIT; Bertec, Columbus, OH, USA). <sentence_start/>Twenty-two markers were placed on the pelvis, thigh, shank, and foot (Leardini et al., <citation rid="B26" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gaitpost.2006.12.018" pmid="17291764" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Out of this dataset, we selected 30 able-bodied volunteers' data (age: 39.7 ± 16.8 years, height: 167.5 ± 11.6 cm, mass: 67.1 ± 11.5 kg, 14 females) at five different walking speeds (1.04 ± 0.12, 1.22 ± 0.15, 1.4 ± 0.17, 1.58 ± 0.2, 1.77 ± 0.21 m/s) with a single trial at each speed. <sentence_start/>Each trial included a single gait cycle, which was defined by two consecutive heel contacts and time-normalized to 101 samples.

We also acquired data for two male unilateral transtibial amputees, both wearing energy-storage-and-return prostheses. <sentence_start/>Amputee 1 was 62 years old, 100 kg heavy, 1.85 m tall, amputated on the left, and wore a Pro-Flex prosthesis (Oessur, Iceland). <sentence_start/>Amputee 2 was 37 years old, 91 kg heavy, 1.75 m tall, amputated on the right, and wore a 1E95 Challenger prosthesis (Ottobock, Germany). <sentence_start/>Each amputee performed multiple trials of level ground walking at self-selected normal and fast speeds. <sentence_start/>Amputee 1 completed eight trials at both normal and fast walking speeds. <sentence_start/>Amputee 2 completed six trials at normal walking speed and four at fast walking speed. <sentence_start/>During each trial, three-dimensional motion data were recorded at 200 Hz using a motion capture system (Vicon Motion Systems, Ltd., UK) with retro-reflective markers, twelve infrared cameras, and data acquisition software (Nexus, Vicon Motion Systems, Ltd., UK). <sentence_start/>The markers were placed over the bony landmarks of the pelvis, thigh, shank, and foot. <sentence_start/>Compared to the marker set for the public dataset, we placed additional non-anatomical markers on the thigh and shank to ensure continuous tracking of these segments in a three-dimensional space. <sentence_start/>For each trial, data from one gait cycle, which was defined by two consecutive heel contacts on the amputated side, was considered for further analysis. <sentence_start/>The recorded marker trajectories were used to calculate θ<italic><sub>hip</sub></italic>, θ<italic><sub>knee</sub></italic>, and θ<italic><sub>shank</sub></italic> on the amputated side. <sentence_start/>This was done using open-source biomechanical modeling software, OpenSim (Delp et al., <citation rid="B11" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/TBME.2007.901024" pmid="18018689" count="1">2007</citation>), and its generic musculoskeletal model (Gait 2392). <sentence_start/>Using the Scaling function of OpenSim and the marker trajectories from a separate static trial, the general model was modified to generate a unique model for each amputee. <sentence_start/>The unique models were used for the Inverse Kinematics and Body Kinematics Analysis functions of OpenSim to calculate θ<italic><sub>hip</sub></italic>, θ<italic><sub>knee</sub></italic>, and θ<italic><sub>shank</sub></italic> within the gait cycle.

The data in the public dataset and the amputee data were both acquired in similar experiments using an infrared-based motion capture system, retro-reflective markers over bony landmarks of the lower extremities, and force plates to record ground reactions forces. <sentence_start/>For both the public dataset and our study, the kinematic and kinetic variables used as input features and model output were generated by performing inverse kinematics and dynamics on the motion capture data with a biomechanical model. <sentence_start/>Although the public dataset was generated for treadmill walking, it has been shown that treadmill gait is qualitatively and quantitatively similar to overground gait (Riley et al., <citation rid="B32" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.gaitpost.2006.07.003" pmid="16905322" count="1">2007</citation>). <sentence_start/>Thus, we consider our experimental data and the public database chosen for our analyses to be comparable.

The able-bodied and amputee data were resampled to 200 samples per gait cycle, and their first derivatives, , and were computed as the numerical difference of angular positions between consecutive samples. <sentence_start/>Although the trials were resampled, the relative patterns of the kinematic and kinetic data during different speeds were preserved. <sentence_start/>The data were low-pass filtered using a Butterworth filter with a cut-off frequency of 6 Hz to remove noise (Little et al., <citation rid="B27" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-3-642-34546-3_112" count="1">2013</citation>; Schurr et al., <citation rid="B33" ref-type="bibr" pmid="28515970" pmcid="PMC5380858" count="1">2017</citation>; Mo et al., <citation rid="B28" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/978-3-030-20476-1_8" count="1">2019</citation>).
2.2. Random Forest Model

Random forest is a supervised ensemble learning model that combines the predictions of multiple estimators called decision trees (Quinlan, <citation rid="B30" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/BF00116251" count="1">1986</citation>; Breiman, <citation rid="B9" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1023/A:1010933404324" count="1">2001</citation>), facilitating better overall performance. <sentence_start/>For regression, the prediction of a random forest model is the average of the predictions of all the decision trees in the ensemble.

In this study, a random forest regression model was trained to map the given θ<italic><sub>hip</sub></italic>, and to the desired θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> and τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic>. <sentence_start/>The working principle of a random forest model can be summarized as follows:

2.4. <sentence_start/>Inter-subject Model

The training and validation procedures of an inter-subject model on able-bodied and amputee subjects are shown in Figure 1. <sentence_start/>The training data was obtained from a publicly-available dataset (Fukuchi et al., <citation rid="B16" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.7717/peerj.4640" pmid="29707431" pmcid="PMC5922232" count="1">2018</citation>). <sentence_start/>The trained models were validated using 5-fold cross-validation: the inter-subject model was trained with data from 24 out of the 30 able-bodied subjects, with the remaining six subjects used for validation. <sentence_start/>For each subject in the training data, trials at five different speeds were used to generalize the model. <sentence_start/>For validation, we compared the inverse kinematics and inverse dynamics derived θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> and τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> against their predicted values.
Figure 1
Block diagram of training and validation procedure of an inter-subject model on able-bodied and amputee subjects.

The trained model was also tested by assessing its predictions based on inputs from the two transtibial amputees. <sentence_start/>The predictions from amputee inputs were compared against the corresponding normative outputs, which were the median of outputs from able-bodied subjects whose walking speeds were within 0.1m/s of that of the amputee's mean walking speed. <sentence_start/>The normative outputs were generated from 24 out of the 30 able-bodied subjects in the same manner as the aforementioned 5-fold cross-validation. <sentence_start/>We have chosen the median for computing the normative values as it is less affected by outlier gait patterns than the mean value. <sentence_start/>The walking speed was estimated from the speed of the pelvis in the walking direction. <sentence_start/>The test output was obtained from the left and right legs of able-bodied subjects for Amputees 1 and 2, respectively.

2.5. <sentence_start/>Subject-Specific Model

4. Discussion

In this study, we examined how the type of training affects the performance of a random forest model when predicting θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> and τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> for 30 able-bodied and two unilateral transtibial amputees from the residual limb kinematics during walking. <sentence_start/>The random forest models were trained using two different approaches: inter-subject and subject-specific. <sentence_start/>The inter-subject approach seeks a generalized input-output relationship for a group of individuals while the subject-specific approach establishes a unique input-output relationship for each individual. <sentence_start/>Since a purely subject-specific model is not possible for the transtibial amputees due to unavailability of the desired reference output (ankle angle and ankle moment), we proposed a modified subject-specific model to map the residual limb kinematics of the amputees to a desired normative trajectory of ankle angle and moment derived from a group of able-bodied individuals.

As expected, the inter-subject model exhibited several flaws in its performance. <sentence_start/>The inaccuracy of the inter-subject model may have been due to the deviation of amputee input features from the able-bodied training data. <sentence_start/>Amputee 1 showed substantial deviations in two of the three most important input features: θ<italic><sub>shank</sub></italic> and (Figure 3), while Amputee 2 showed less deviation for the three most important input features (Figure 4), and this may have resulted in the relatively inaccurate prediction of θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> for Amputee 1 (Figure 8). <sentence_start/>Also, it was observed that the inclusion of the anthropometric inputs generally impaired prediction accuracy, most probably due to inconsistent relationships between the anthropometric inputs and the predicted variables. <sentence_start/>This may have been due to our dataset structure which contained only one trial per walking speed for each subject. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the effect of anthropometric inputs should be further investigated on a dataset that contains more trials of the same speed levels or in a dataset where inter-speed variation for each subject is lower.

The subject-specific models performed significantly better than the inter-subject model for both able-bodied individuals and amputees. <sentence_start/>For both the able-bodied individuals and the two amputees, high prediction accuracy was obtained for both θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> and τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> for all the tested speed levels (Figures 10, 11). <sentence_start/>Using the kinematic input features or the important input features gave comparable performance. <sentence_start/>This finding indicates that subject-specific models may be more ideal for devising a potential control strategy for an intelligent prosthesis than the inter-subject models.

One of the most important results from our study is the ability of the subject-specific model to generalize its learning to different untrained walking speeds with high accuracy. <sentence_start/>For a real-world implementation of a control scheme using the proposed model, this is a very important characteristic. <sentence_start/>We tested the speed generalization capability of the subject-specific model for three untrained speeds for able-bodied subjects and one untrained speed for each of the amputee subjects. <sentence_start/>The results suggest that if the model is trained for a certain speed, it can generalize this learning up to a speed difference of 0.4 m/s.

It was also shown in our study that, using only the important features selected by the random forest as input, it was possible to obtain similar or higher accuracy of the predicted output variables compared to using all the available input features. <sentence_start/>Here, we also point out that our models did not have any physiological basis. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the important features are not necessarily the most important determinants of gait. <sentence_start/>Instead, the important input features are those variables that most effectively discerned the outputs for model learning. <sentence_start/>Specifically, the important input features are used preferentially by random forests to split at a given node and result in larger variance reduction of the output values on the left and the right nodes compared to other features. <sentence_start/>It can be interpreted that, important features define an input-output relation with minimal overlap in input values for different values of the output. <sentence_start/>The features marked as the most important were different for inter-subject and subject-specific models, which we assume is due to the difference in the data variations in training approaches. <sentence_start/>However, θ<italic><sub>shank</sub></italic> remained important for both approaches. <sentence_start/>The large standard deviations of feature importance for subject-specific models trained for able-bodied subjects indicated large inter-individual differences in relative feature importance. <sentence_start/>This could be due to the inter-individual variations in gait patterns of able-bodied subjects. <sentence_start/>More interestingly, the features which were determined as important were consistent between the two amputee subjects. <sentence_start/>Although the input features of the amputees deviate from each other, this similarity may be partly due to the training approach we followed to map the amputee's input features to normative outputs. <sentence_start/>A limitation of the feature importance calculation using random forest's mean decrease in impurity is that the correlated features are given similar but reduced relative importance. <sentence_start/>However, this did not affect the prediction performance of our models while using Important input features, since the importance of these features summed to at least 85%. <sentence_start/>Therefore, our results suggest that feature selection could result in high accuracy while reducing the input dimension thereby potentially increasing model efficiency for real-time applications.

We have chosen a very heterogeneous dataset with respect to subjects, trials, and speeds for inferring the able-bodied model inputs and outputs. <sentence_start/>This was done to simulate a real-world scenario to some extent, where the gait cycles across trials and speeds might not be highly homogeneous. <sentence_start/>We may consider the heterogeneity across subjects and speeds as simulating variations that require the model to be robust. <sentence_start/>Thus, we have tested most of our training and validation conditions in adverse and minimal data conditions where we had only one trial per speed for each of five speeds for thirty able-bodied subjects. <sentence_start/>We believe that much better performance of the models could be achieved if a more homogeneous dataset or a dataset with more trials from the same speed level would be considered. <sentence_start/>Also, our models were based on pattern recognition. <sentence_start/>Therefore, the actual or the physical meaning of the predictor input variables were not necessary as long as the relative patterns were preserved. <sentence_start/>For example, the first derivatives were calculated as the numerical difference between the consecutive angular positions without time normalization.

The performance of the subject specific training approach was comparable to other state-of-the-art machine learning regression algorithms used in previous studies for gait variable predictions. <sentence_start/>For example, Eslamy and Schilling (<citation rid="B15" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/BIOROB.2018.8487213" count="1">2018</citation>) reported an <italic>R</italic><sup>2</sup> score above 0.92 using Gaussian process regression for ankle kinematic prediction for the trained speed levels. <sentence_start/>Ardestani et al. (<citation rid="B2" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.eswa.2013.11.003" count="1">2014</citation>) used a wavelet neural network for prediction for lower extremity moments during walking and obtained a correlation coefficient, ρ > 0.94, and <italic>NRMSE</italic> < 10%. <sentence_start/>Dey et al. (<citation rid="B12" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1109/ICORR.2019.8779445" pmid="31374717" count="1">2019</citation>) reported <italic>R</italic><sup>2</sup> values of 0.98 for θ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> and 0.97 for τ<italic><sub>ankle</sub></italic> using support vector regression for level ground walking at self-selected normal speeds. <sentence_start/>However, the difference in selection of input features, difference in datasets, amount of data used, and different performance quantification measures makes a direct comparison with other studies difficult. <sentence_start/>Nevertheless, none of these studies have attempted prediction of gait variables for amputee subjects where the impaired gait patterns and incomplete user specific training data poses challenges for using the machine learning regression algorithms for active prosthesis control. <sentence_start/>We believe that our study is a necessary initial step in this direction.

The proposed random forest approach could be potentially used to devise a high-level control strategy for active ankle prostheses which could predict the ankle angles or moments continuously during level-ground walking at varying speeds. <sentence_start/>A low-level controller could take the output of the high-level controller as input and directly generate the required moments (for torque control) or angles (for position control) or both (for a composite torque-position control during stance and swing phase, respectively). <sentence_start/>The input features used in this study could be obtained using wearable sensors like goniometers or IMUs which measure joint or limb rotations in real-time. <sentence_start/>Since the inputs are required only from the ipsilateral side, the non-prosthetic side does not need to be instrumented.

There were a few limitations to our study. <sentence_start/>First, the data used in our study was acquired from motion capture experiments. <sentence_start/>However, for real-life locomotive conditions, the data need to be acquired using wearable sensors which may contain artifacts that were not taken into consideration here. <sentence_start/>Second, the subject specific models for amputees were trained with data acquired while the amputees walked with a passive prosthesis. <sentence_start/>Therefore, adaptability of the model to changes in the prosthetic set-up constitutes a crucial part of future studies. <sentence_start/>Using the predicted angles/moments for controlling the active prosthesis might also in turn alter the input patterns to some extent. <sentence_start/>Thus, imparting robustness to the control model remains another focus of our future study. <sentence_start/>This might call for an iterative online training of the model to adapt to new training inputs to enhance model efficiency. <sentence_start/>Furthermore, future studies should also focus on evaluating the proposed subject-specific model on a larger pool of amputee subjects and on different locomotion modes. <sentence_start/>Finally, the proposed approach should be validated on online experiments to control an active prosthesis.
5. <sentence_start/>Conclusion

We investigated the feasibility of two different approaches-subject-specific and inter-subject-for training a random forest model using incomplete amputee-specific training data for predicting the ankle angle and ankle moment during level-ground walking. <sentence_start/>We found that a random forest subject-specific model predicted the required normative ankle motion with up to three times lower errors than an inter-subject model and could generalize its learning to different speeds up to a difference of 0.4 m/s from the speed which it was trained. <sentence_start/>These results are promising and suggest that the proposed random-forest based model could be used to device a robust control strategy for an intelligent prosthetic ankle, which can adapt to its specific user at varying speeds and produce the required ankle angle or moment similar to an able-bodied walking gait. <sentence_start/>The general approach could also be useful in other fields with incomplete training data, e.g., other human-computer interfaces like upper limb prosthetics, assistive robotics, e.g., cyborg and bionic technologies.
